# Executive summary

This report evaluates Keir's proposed log-scale retransformation correction
across the six shortlisted Yang–Zhang volatility models. For each model, the
target is fit as $Z_t=\log(Y_t)$, then forecasts are returned to the volatility
scale using

$$
\widehat{Y}_{t+1}
= \exp\left(\widehat{\mu}_{t+1}
  + \frac{1}{2}\widehat{\sigma}_{t+1}^{\,2}\right).
$$

The correction estimates the conditional mean if log-scale forecast errors are
conditionally normal. By contrast, $\exp(\widehat{\mu}_{t+1})$ estimates the
conditional median. The experiment used 761 sequential holdout targets from
2023-06-02 through 2026-11-10, with zero failed fits across all six models.

The transformation did **not** resolve the larger Q5 errors. On the exact
baseline-Q5 dates, raw residual variance rose for five models and fell by only
0.2% for HGB. None of the paired overall MAE or RMSE differences was
significant at 5% after Holm adjustment. Treat the results as an exploratory
comparison on a previously used holdout, not as evidence of a winning model.

The team has also tested a subsequent Keir/Enoch proposal: segmented parameter
estimation. The 80th-percentile extreme-state experiments gave worse
point losses than the unsegmented baselines in the available
761-target holdout. They therefore do not overturn the log-transformation
finding; the next diagnostic step is to examine residual timing and identify
the source of the remaining large misses before choosing a final model.

# Data and model implementation

The target is the unannualized daily volatility, the square root of the
two-observation Yang–Zhang variance estimate from LSEG's generic COMEX gold
futures series `GCc1`. The chronological sample has 3,040 training targets and
761 test targets. At each test origin, fitting used the initial training
sample and only previously observed test targets; the target being forecast
was excluded from its own history.

The six models were:

| Model | Log-scale specification and variance used for correction |
|:--|:--|
| GARCH(1,1) | AR(1) mean and GARCH(1,1) conditional variance, fit to log volatility |
| EGARCH(1,1) | AR(1) mean and EGARCH(1,1) conditional variance, fit to log volatility |
| Range GARCH-X | AR(1) log-volatility mean; OHLC range enters the conditional-variance equation; Gaussian quasi-likelihood |
| EGARCH-X | Selected DXY and gold implied-volatility predictors remain in the ARX mean; EGARCH conditional variance |
| HAR-X (OHLC) | Existing HAR lag and predictor regression on log volatility; training OLS residual variance |
| HGB (OHLC) | Existing log-target boosting specification; training in-sample residual variance; random seed 42 |

HAR-X and HGB already model log volatility in the existing pipeline. For
these models, this experiment applies the variance correction; the other four
models are refit on the log target. GARCH-family corrections use the fitted
one-step conditional log variance. Regression-model corrections use
training-sample log-residual variance. HGB's in-sample residual variance may
understate its prediction error.

# Overall holdout performance

Errors are defined as **actual minus forecast**; positive mean error denotes
under-forecasting. Metrics are shown in units of $10^{-3}$ volatility.

| Model | MAE: baseline → corrected | RMSE: baseline → corrected | Mean error: baseline → corrected |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| GARCH(1,1) | 2.912 → 2.930 | 5.025 → 5.036 | 0.644 → 0.420 |
| EGARCH(1,1) | 2.912 → 2.945 | 5.022 → 5.115 | 0.621 → 0.540 |
| Range GARCH-X | 2.914 → 2.930 | 5.037 → 5.036 | 0.716 → 0.420 |
| EGARCH-X | 2.833 → 2.855 | 4.860 → 4.902 | 0.321 → 0.086 |
| HAR-X (OHLC) | 2.758 → 2.825 | 5.625 → 5.852 | 0.623 → −0.060 |
| HGB (OHLC) | 2.423 → 2.437 | 4.736 → 4.657 | 0.821 → 0.386 |

The mean bias moved closer to zero for all six models, but the point-loss
changes were small and mixed. HGB's RMSE decreased slightly; its Holm-adjusted
DM p-value was 0.058 with Newey–West bandwidth 1 and 0.142 with bandwidth 4.
Neither is below 0.05. No model's overall paired MAE or RMSE difference was
significant after adjustment.

# Q5 residual variance

The first variance comparison below holds Q5 membership fixed to the baseline
model's highest forecast quintile, so both forecast versions are evaluated on
the same 152 dates. Variances are in units of $10^{-5}$ volatility squared.
The last column reports the corrected forecast's own Q5/Q1 error-variance
ratio, with quintiles ranked within that model over the holdout.

| Model | Baseline Q5 variance | Corrected variance on same dates | Variance change | Corrected model Q5/Q1 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| GARCH(1,1) | 7.433 | 7.543 | +1.5% | 9.65 |
| EGARCH(1,1) | 7.437 | 7.839 | +5.4% | 9.90 |
| Range GARCH-X | 7.441 | 7.543 | +1.4% | 9.65 |
| EGARCH-X | 7.288 | 7.600 | +4.3% | 15.53 |
| HAR-X (OHLC) | 11.413 | 12.881 | +12.9% | 20.93 |
| HGB (OHLC) | 7.038 | 7.024 | −0.2% | 13.27 |

Thus, the log transformation and mean correction did not make high-forecast
errors less dispersed. The Q5/Q1 ratios remain substantially above one. The
variance changes are descriptive; no separate statistical test of Q5 variance
differences was performed.

# Paired forecast-loss tests

For each model, corrected forecasts were compared with that model's existing
baseline on the same target dates. Tests use absolute and squared errors,
Newey–West bandwidths 1 and 4, the Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold correction, and
Holm adjustment across the six model comparisons within each loss/bandwidth
family. Negative transformed-minus-baseline loss favors the corrected
forecast.

No overall comparison is statistically significant at the 5% level after
Holm adjustment. The closest result is HGB squared error: adjusted p-values
are 0.058 (bandwidth 1) and 0.142 (bandwidth 4). Full statistics are in the
[DM results CSV](../outputs/samuel/stage3_q5/log_transform/log_transform_dm_tests.csv).

# Segmented parameter estimation

Keir proposed a segmented approach when $y_t$ or $y_{t-1}$ is extreme:
use a second set of parameters for that state rather than applying one
universal parameter set. Two training-only 80th-percentile triggers were
implemented:

- **Forecast trigger:** fit a pilot model using the full history available
  at the origin. Use the normal or extreme parameter set according to whether
  the pilot forecast exceeds the training-history threshold.
- **Lagged-target trigger:** use the latest observed $y_{t-1}$ to select the
  normal or extreme parameter set.

In both designs, the threshold is defined from the expanding training history
only. The selected parameter set is refit on observations in the matching
lagged-realized-volatility regime. The parameter sample excludes future
targets, so this is a no-look-ahead implementation. GARCH, EGARCH, range
GARCH-X, EGARCH-X, HAR-X, and HGB are each tested under both triggers.

| Model | Baseline MAE/RMSE | Best segmented MAE/RMSE | Better trigger |
|:--|--:|--:|:--|
| GARCH(1,1) | 0.002912 / 0.005025 | 0.003238 / 0.005923 | Forecast |
| EGARCH(1,1) | 0.002912 / 0.005022 | 0.003204 / 0.005758 | Forecast |
| Range GARCH-X | 0.002914 / 0.005037 | 0.003238 / 0.005912 | Lagged target |
| EGARCH-X | 0.002833 / 0.004860 | 0.003117 / 0.005536 | Forecast |
| HAR-X (OHLC) | 0.002711 / 0.005091 | 0.002879 / 0.005169 | Lagged target |
| HGB (OHLC) | 0.002418 / 0.004767 | 0.002680 / 0.005124 | Forecast |

All 12 model-trigger combinations produced forecasts on all 761 holdout
dates, with zero fit failures. Their MAE and RMSE are nevertheless above the
reported unsegmented baselines, except for the range GARCH-X RMSE comparison:
the lagged-target segmented RMSE is 0.0059126 versus the baseline 0.005037
shown in the table. This is not an improvement in the table's MAE/RMSE
pair and is not a model-superiority result.

The segmented forecasts also changed the sign of average mean error. The
reported segment biases are negative:

| Model/trigger | Segmented mean error |
|:--|--:|
| GARCH, forecast trigger | +0.000960 |
| GARCH, lagged-target trigger | +0.000780 |
| EGARCH, forecast trigger | +0.000915 |
| EGARCH, lagged-target trigger | +0.000779 |
| Range GARCH-X, forecast trigger | +0.001027 |
| Range GARCH-X, lagged-target trigger | +0.000841 |
| EGARCH-X, forecast trigger | +0.000383 |
| EGARCH-X, lagged-target trigger | +0.000338 |
| HAR-X, forecast trigger | +0.000983 |
| HAR-X, lagged-target trigger | +0.000936 |
| HGB, forecast trigger | +0.000965 |
| HGB, lagged-target trigger | +0.000829 |

The saved segmented summary uses forecast-minus-actual bias. In this report,
the values above are reversed to the project's actual-minus-forecast sign,
so the positive values indicate average under-forecasting. This is a
regime-estimation result that deserves attention, but it does not reverse
the fact that the segmented solutions have larger MAE/RMSE than their
baselines.

# Residual timing and source of error

The log transformation and segmentation experiments change target
transformation or parameter membership; they do not identify why the largest
misses occur. The next analysis should therefore plot forecast residuals
against calendar date, forecast level, lagged volatility, and realized
volatility, while retaining the largest individual misses.

The existing residual-diagnostics artifacts already show the residual path
over time and residual dispersion versus forecast level:

- [Residuals over the test period](figures/model_residual_diagnostics/forecast_errors_over_time.png)
- [Residuals versus forecast level](figures/model_residual_diagnostics/forecast_errors_vs_forecast.png)
- [Joint-predictor residual-diagnostics report](yang-zhang-selected-residual-diagnostics.qmd)

The source of error should be evaluated separately as:

1. **A common target/recording episode:** check whether all models miss the
   same dates, especially abrupt regime changes.
2. **Model specification:** compare whether the model underpredicts a level
   term, a predictor term, or a conditional-variance term.
3. **Data timing:** verify target and predictor availability at each origin.
4. **Dependence:** account for overlapping Yang–Zhang windows and serial
   dependence before treating residual patterns as independent evidence.
5. **Heavy tails and regime shifts:** separate an isolated-outlier explanation
   from a persistent change in conditional volatility.

This residual-source exercise should report dates and common miss episodes
before drawing a limitation or model-selection conclusion. It should not
use future target-window values or future thresholds.

# Relation to the Student-t and residual-source work

The team is also preparing Normal-versus-Student-t comparisons for the
six candidates. That experiment addresses innovation-tail behavior; it does
not replace the residual-source diagnostic above. A Student-t likelihood can
change predictive intervals and estimated degrees of freedom, while a residual
timing or regime analysis asks whether the point forecast systematically
misses particular dates or regimes.

The existing distribution-comparison report should be used as the formal
Student-t companion:

- [Normal and Student-t Yang–Zhang forecasts](yang-zhang-distribution-comparison.qmd)

The final model discussion should combine, rather than merge, three distinct
findings: point-loss performance, predictive density/calibration, and the
source and timing of residual misses. No result in this log or segmentation
experiment establishes a final model decision.

# Limitations and interpretation

- The retransformation formula is exact under a conditional normal
  log-error model. Normality has not been established for HAR-X or HGB.
- HAR-X uses training OLS residual variance; HGB uses in-sample residual
  variance, which may be optimistic.
- The holdout has been used in prior model analysis. Forecast-ranked Q5 is
  retrospective, and adjacent two-observation Yang–Zhang targets overlap.
- Paired tests concern overall loss, not Q5 variance. The same-holdout
  comparisons are exploratory and do not establish causal effects or durable
  superiority.
- Segmentation uses the previously examined holdout and a training-history
  80th-percentile threshold. It has no paired significance tests and should
  not be presented as a deployable rule or a superior model.
- The segmented results have 761 successful observations for each of 12
  model-trigger combinations, but this sample is not independent of the
  model-development decisions already made on the holdout.
- Lower mean error does not by itself establish full forecast calibration.
